scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Once a vital tool for survival and resistance among enslaved populations, the Calenda evolved from a Kongo combat tradition into a diverse array of Caribbean stick-fighting and performance arts.
on_screen: Title card: Calenda (Kalinda) · Trinidad and Tobago, Haiti, France (Caribbean territories) · 1720s

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The tradition originated in the 1720s, brought to the Caribbean by enslaved people from the Kingdom of Kongo.
It served as a martial art and performance, later evolving into a central component of Caribbean Carnival culture and Haitian Vodou ceremonies.
on_screen: Map: Trinidad and Tobago, Haiti, France (Caribbean territories) · Caribbean

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Calenda is performed during Carnival, Vodou ceremonies, and as a competitive martial art.
Historically, it served as a means of entertainment for enslaved people and a tool for resistance during colonial rule.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance involves stick-fighting and mimetic combat.
In historical variations, dancers jump over water bottles while brandishing sticks, requiring precise footwork to avoid spilling water.
The movement is rhythmic and often performed within a circular arena called a gayelle.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is driven by call-and-response chants led by a 'chantwell' or 'chantuelle.' These songs, known as 'lavways,' provide the rhythmic foundation for the fighters and are considered precursors to modern calypso.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The 'chantwell' (or chantuelle) is the primary figure, responsible for leading the rhythmic chants that accompany the fighters.
Variants include 'Mayolè' and 'Ladja baton' in Guadeloupe and Martinique, 'Tire machèt' in Haiti, 'Kokobalé' in Puerto Rico, and 'stick-licking' or 'stick science' in Barbados.
The tradition descends from combat dances of the Kingdom of Kongo, adapted through the transatlantic slave trade into Afro-Caribbean martial arts.

narration: In Haiti, the dance is performed during Vodou ceremonies; practitioners should respect the sanctity of these spaces.
